Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday last

Man-Power-Labour Priorities
as recorded on page 3467 of Hansard, the hon. member for Danforth inquired about labour priorities. I would like to make the following answer. Labour priorities are established for all industries in the priorities division of the labour supply branch, Department of Labour, by the interdepartmental labour priorities committee, consisting of representatives of the wartime prices and trade board, Department of Munitions and Supply and selective service. The priority assigned to an industry is based on the relative essentiality of its normal production. Many firms normally producing relatively less essential goods change over to the production of war materials and must be assigned a priority rating in accordance with the assessment of the essentiality of their new activities.
Labour priorities are confidential and are not disclosed, even to the firms concerned. Firms may make application for special priority consideration through their wartime prices and trade board administrator, or directly to the priorities division of the Department of Labour. All applications and claims are investigated by the wartime prices and trade board and Department of Munitions and Supply representatives and, when justified, are presented to the interdepartmental labour priorities committee for their consideration.
May I ask the minister why these are so confidential?

Because the relative
importance of industries may change from [DOT]day to day. That is the reason. I think my hon. friend will agree that it is just as well that it should be kept confidential. That is the considered judgment of all the agencies that are concerned with the question of priorities for industrial operations.

I can quite understand the minister's position. That is one side [DOT]of the argument. The other is the possibility that observance of confidence in the matter might be carried to the point of abuse. I am not suggesting that this exists, but in any event the possibility of its arising is there.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. I hold in my hand an application form for renewal of a passport. This came to me by chance. I tried to get a few copies of these application forms from the passport office because everybody knows it is absolutely necessary for members of parliament to have some of them on hand for the use of constituents who desire to renew their passports; but I was informed by the passport office that I could have none, and that they should be asked for direct by the applicant. Surely if this is done as a matter of economy, it is, as we say in French, une economie de bout de chandelle. If the government wants to economize, it could save much more by economizing on stationery, dispensing with the large envelopes that come to members of parliament with just a short letter inside.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

I do not mind saying to my hon. friend, as I intended to say the other day, that while the passport office is making its rule rigid, it has from its point of view good reasons for so doing. I myself feel that possibly there might be a measure of concession made to members of parliament. The department's purpose is to effect economies and at the same time to maintain in the use of these forms a certain security which is regarded by our government and by the United States government as important. However, I am not sorry that my hon. friend has brought the matter up, and I shall have another discussion with the officials of the department about it. Even ministers themselves sometimes find it difficult to get things done in their own departments that they themselves might wish to do.

I have personally taken up with Madame Chiang Kai-shek what she might find it possible to do in the way of speaking before hon. members of the house and over the radio, and have since taken up the question whether it wouldi be possible for her to speak outdoors. Madame Chiang Kai-shek herself would prefer to speak indoors, and also to make just one address. To permit of the address being broadcast

I am sure that arrangements can be made for having loud speakers on parliament hill, and I have no doubt that if the citizens are gathered there Madame Chiang Kai-shek will be only too happy to make an appearance 'before them, but I am quite sure she would wish to be spared having to deliver a second address.

War Appropriation-Supplies

Over the past three and a half years I have made reports to the house from time to time on the production, programme. These were reports of progress towards objectives yet to be attained. It will be recalled that there were always one or two items in the programme which were giving us trouble either because of difficulty of design, the need for elaborate tooling, or shortages of critical materials and components. I am now able to report that certain of our major objectives have been reached. Late in 1942 we were delivering in substantial quantities every item of war equipment for which we had received orders in the first two and a half years of the war. Every week we are launching six or more vessels, either escort, cargo or patrol. Every week we are turning out 80 planes. Every week our automobile factories produce 4,000 motor vehicles and 450 fighting vehicles. Every week our gun plants make 940 heavy guns or mountings, and our small arms plants turn out 13,000 smaller weapons. Every week our ammunition factories make 525,000 rounds of heavy ammunition and 25,000,000 rounds of small arms ammunition. Every week our chemicals and explosive industry has an output of 10,000 tons. Every week our factories produce $4,000,000 worth of instruments and communications equipment. We have launched 500 ships and delivered 8,000 aircraft. We have delivered 475,000 motor vehicles and 21,300 fighting vehicles. We have delivered 55,500 heavy guns or mountings and 630,000 small weapons. We have produced 800,000 tons of chemicals and explosives. We have produced instruments and communications equipment to the value of $160,000,000. These are some of the highlights of a programme which includes almost every type of equipment and supply needed in modern warfare. The total dollar value of our deliveries to date is over $4,500,000,000. We estimate employment in war industry at upwards of 900,000 men and women.
I mentioned a moment ago that certain of our targets had been attained. This does not mean that there will be any slackening of the over-all effort, but rather a change in emphasis. Some programmes will be reduced, others will be expanded. There are some rather drastic reductions in ground army stores on the one hand, but on the other greatly increased demands for naval vessels, guns and equipment, combat aircraft and radar equipment. Before receiving notice of changes in programme, our over-all production programme for the fiscal year 1943-44 totalled 3 billion, 653 million dollars. We are now able to estimate the revised programme at

3 billion, 425 million dollars, or a shrinkage of approximately 6 per cent. Of this shrinkage approximately 30 million dollars represents reductions in defence construction projects, leaving slightly less than 200 million dollars or a 5^ per cent net reduction in the production programme. Because we realized that changes in programme were inevitable in war production, we have maintained a high degree of flexibility in the planning of our production facilities, which now permits us to make the changes necessary with a minimum of inconvenience.
I will comment briefly now on each item of the programme, giving the accomplishment to date and indicating what changes will be made, either by way of reduction or expansion.
Ammunition. We have created a great ammunition industry in Canada. More than 38 million rounds of heavy ammunition have come from our factories. Complete filled rounds of this heavy ammunition are now produced at a rate of 525,000 rounds a week.
At the close of 1942 we were making 28 types of shells of 15 different calibres, ranging from the 40 millimeter quick-firing shell to the 7-2 howitzer. So far this year three types have gone out of production. Of the remaining 25 types, two will be increased in output, others will be produced at the current rate, and others will be reduced.
Some cuts in production will take place at once, but wherever possible any necessary reductions in the programme will be made over a period of months and should cause a minimum dislocation of manpower.
All told, there are nearly 50 plants engaged in making shells alone. There are scores of other plants producing components, including 12 types of fuses, 14 types of cartridge cases, two types of gaines, six kinds of primers, two types of depth charges, ten types of trench mortar bombs, pyrotechnics of 70 different kinds, as well as practice bombs, anti-tank mines, rifle grenades.
Components. As the output of shells declines, so the production of cartridge cases, fuses, primers and gaines will also be reduced. However, all of the cartridge case manufacturing capacity thus released will be diverted' to making additional cartridge cases for the United States. Over-all production will' decline. Some plants can be converted to the manufacture of other types of equipment, but this is not possible in every case.
Chemicals and Explosives. The vast Canadian chemicals and explosives production is supervised by Allied War Supplies Limited. This crown company has under its control 40

War Appropriation-Supplies
different projects, 34 of which have come into full operation. Of the 18 major projects on the list, three are mammoth ammunitionfilling developments, three are making explosives, two are fuse-filling undertakings, and the others are chemicals producers. Total employment in these factories is in excess of 50,000 men and women.
The various Canadian chemicals and explosives projects under the administration of Allied War Supplies cover an area equal to that of the city of Montreal. The largest, are the shell-filling ' plants, but on one explosives project alone the capital expenditure runs to 18 million dollars.
Great Britain and the allied nations have relied heavily upon us for this production.
Our present production of chemicals and explosives is running at a rate of 10,000 tons a week. The total quantity turned out to date is in excess of 800,000 tons. One of these products is the most powerful explosive developed anywhere during the present war. The production of this valuable and secret explosive is being increased.
As our heavy ammunition programme recedes from its peak, due to decreased requirements, production of certain explosives and propellants will also be reduced.
Small arms ammunition. A tremendous production job has been accomplished in small arms ammunition. In 1940 we made only three types, to a value of 4J million dollars. Now we are making 20 main types, ranging in calibre from -22 to 20 mm., having a value of 23 million dollars for the four months from January 1 to the end of April of this year.
The 9 mm., bullet, used in the Sten carbine, can be cited as one example of a lowered target. The future objective has merely been lowered so that the present production figure will be tripled instead of quadrupled.
Much planning remains to be done before anything more definite can be said regarding revision of the small arms ammunition programme, because these changes must be made on the basis of advices received only a few days ago. In the meantime, we are turning out more than 25 million rounds a week in plants and arsenals employing 30,000 people, half of them women. The government arsenal at Quebec is the model on this continent for this type of production, both in efficiency of operation and quality and quantity of production.
Guns. In the production of heavy guns and small arms, we have achieved mass output on a constantly rising scale. Toward
the end of 1942 our monthly ordnance output was greater than it had been for the entire 1941 year.
More than one-fifth of the total government investment in war plants has been allocated to the production of guns and small arms.
We are making twelve types of heavy ordnance, and 16 types of carriages and mountings, in Canadian shops. To date we have produced 55,500 guns, gun barrels or mountings. Our weekly production rate is now 940 units-570 guns and gun barrels and 370 mountings. Merchant ships and combat vessels made in Canadian yards can now be equipped with Canadian-made guns. Our field artillery, anti-aircraft guns, our tank and anti-tank guns are being shipped overseas for service on all fronts.
We are now engaged in revising some of our gun schedules downwards. The items most likely to be affected are the 3-7 and Bofors anti-aircraft guns and the 6-pounder anti-tank gun. The scheduled production of 3-7 and 40 mm. Bofors AA guns will carry on at a reduced scale to the end of 1944. The plant making the 6-pounder carriage is being converted to the manufacture of 20 mm. Universal mountings for the army and single 20 mm. mountings for the navy.
There are eight major plants and scores of subcontractors operating on small arms contract. Our output of small arms in 1942 increased 1,300 per cent over 1941. We have turned out 630,000 small arms to date and present production is at the rate of 13,000 units a week. These include rifles, carbines, anti-tank rifles, smoke dischargers, bomb throwers, two types of trench mortars, and four types of machine guns.
In line with the changing picture of our overall production programme, there will also be adjustments in the small arms schedule.
Maximum output of the Bren gun, 8,000 per month, will be reached this month and will be maintained at that rate until the end of 1944. Original schedule for the No. 4 army rifle, Canadian version of Lee-Enfield, which is being produced in the government-owned and operated plant, Small Arms Limited, was doubled during the past year, and our present output is now in excess of 34,000 a month. Production of this weapon will be increased to better than 40,000 a month.
Production of the Sten, which is now at peak, will be slightly reduced from the maximum planned-10,000 a month. Present orders on hand for Vickers, -5-inch naval machine guns, training rifles, and 2-inch trench mortars are sufficient to carry us into 1944.

Motorized Equipment. One of the most important contributions Canadian industry has made to the war is our output of fighting vehicles and motor transport. It is generally agreed that a major factor in the victories of the British armies in Africa was the quality and reliability of the motorized equipment they had at their disposal in the Egyptian, Libyan and Tunisian campaigns. More than 36 per cent of the motorized equipment

throughout the entire middle east if of Canadian make. Fifty per cent of the load-carrying vehicles used by Montgomery's victorious Eighth Army were Canadian made.
Soon, very soon, the 500,000th motor vehicle will roll from the assembly line of one of our automobile plants. We are turning out these military vehicles, as distinguished from fighting units, in more than 100 different types at a rate of 4,000 a week. Our present production of fighting vehicles, including tanks, ruus to 450 a week, for a present total of more than 24,000 units.
So highly are our Canadian-made military vehicles rated that this programme of ground equipment production is to be continued at its present peak capacity.
Through our army engineering design branch, constant changes and improvements have been effected in the motorized transport and fighting vehicles made in Canada. Our designers have achieved remarkable results in improving the quality, performance, and utility of mechanized units. The Canadian "dry pin track" for instance, has just been approved for production. Developed by our own design branch, it is a tank track which not only gives better performance than any other type in use to-day, but can be made more economically than any other. The lessons learned in active theatres of war are being steadily applied. The motorized units we are sending overseas to-day are more serviceable, better built, and more economically manufactured than the units of a year ago. New models are constantly going into production.
Tanks. We have just completed our Valentine tank programme. The total production- 1,400-has gone to Russia. Recalling our difficulties in the early stages of this programme, I am able to say that the last tank was delivered exactly on shedule. The plant has been converted to the production of engines and components for the escort vessel programme. We are approaching the end of our contract for Ram tanks. Over 1,700 have been produced. Our tank arsenal is now producing self-propelling gun mounts, and will shortly go into production on the M-4 tank. This type is now standard for the United States, British and Canadian armies.
Instruments and Communications. In the field of instruments and communications we have made remarkable progress. We have produced intricate instruments to the extent of $160 million and the 1943 production will reach the $250 million mark. They are now being produced at a rate of $4-3 million a week.

Three new industries have been developed in Canada to meet the demands of the radio industry, the output of Which has expanded sixteenfold since the beginning of the war. They are a dynamotor industry, a ceramic insulation industry, and a crystal industry.
We have become a major source of united nations supply in this field. Canadian invention is responsible for seven major developments in the production of signals equipment. Ranging from a "talkie-walkie" set which one man can operate as easily as a cradle phone, to a super-highpower field wireless station with a radius of more than 100 miles. These products of original Canadian design have so impressed our allies that large orders have been placed in Canada for tens of millions of dollars worth of this equipment.
All the communication devices for Canadian tanks, ships, planes, and motorized vehicles are being produced in volume in this country. These are the artificial eyes and ears of our armed forces. Optical instruments by the tens of thousands have been produced to date by Research Enterprises Limited, a government-owned company producing a great variety of intricate equipment such as prismatic gunsights, clinometers, periscopes, range-finders, dial sights and cathode tubes. This company, which employs 6,800 people, is working on orders for radio and optical equipment totalling more than 130 million dollars.
Aircraft. To date Canada has produced 8,000 planes. Aircraft are now coming from our factories at the rate of 80 a week in nine types. We are now passing through an intermediate stage, entering production of new trainer types and just achieving production of combat planes such as the Lancaster and Mosquito, which presented very special and difficult production problems. The low production point arising from the change in models has now been passed. Production figures will steadily increase. While we have had ups and downs in our monthly planned production, actually the total poundage of planes produced has steadily mounted since the middle of 1940, when we were producing only two planes a week.
The four types of trainer craft upon which the industry is now engaged are the Fairchild Cornell, an elementary trainer; the North American Harvard, a single-engined advanced trainer; the Canadian Anson, regarded as the best twin-engined advanced trainer in the world, which is 'being produced under the supervision of the government-owned company, Federal Aircraft Limited, and the Bristol Bolingbroke, a twin-engined reconnaissance bomber and gunnery trainer.
The service types are the PBY-5A Catalina, a coastal reconnaissance amphibian; the Lancaster, mightiest four-engined long-range bomber in the world, being produced in the government-owned and operated plant Victory Aircraft Limited; the Curtiss Helldiver, navy dive bomber, and the famous Mosquito, fast twin-engined fighter bomber. In addition to these, we are also producing the Noorduyn Norseman, the only all-Canadian designed plane on the list, regarded-as the best single-engined all-round transport type plane yet designed.
Two of the planes I have mentioned have yet to come into production. Design modifications have held up the dive bomber programme, but these have now been cleared, and the first Lancaster, biggest and most ambitious job ever undertaken by the Canadian aircraft industry, is expected to be test-flown within a few weeks.
The Canadian aircraft industry, and plants in component manufacture, now employ more than 100,000 workers. More than 25 per cent of these employees are women. Because we are increasing our production, the aircraft industry will in future be able to absorb all workers, not required by the armed services and in high priority shipbuilding, who were hitherto employed on those programmes which are to be curtailed.
In addition to the production of new aircraft, Canada has established an aircraft overhaul industry to service the thousands of planes now operating in the dominion. Thirty special plants are located strategically across the dominion, to make regular engine overhauls, to take care of airframe reconditioning, and to rebuild damaged planes. These plants recondition and replace into service 200 planes and 800 engines every month.
In any assessment of our aircraft record, two points are basic; first, every single plane we are building today is the accepted leader in its class; and, second, the quality of workmanship and the methods employed in the manufacture of Canadian planes are unexcelled.
Cargo Ship Building. During the twenty years before the outbreak of this war, Canada built not one seagoing merchant ship. Our present record in shipbuilding, therefore, is all the more remarkable in that it represents the achievement of what is virtually a new major industry.
Last month we launched 19 cargo vessels from Canadian yards.
By the end of May we had achieved a total of 168 freighters launched under our cargo vessel programme. Of these, 141 had been

delivered by the end of May. All but four of these are 10,000 ton vessels. The others are 4,700 tonners.
Roughly one-half of our overall commitments for shipbuilding in Canada, which total one billion dollars, will be spent on cargo ship construction.
Freighters delivered, under construction, or on order, total more than 300, of which 90 per cent are 10,000 ton ships.
The 43,000 workers in the 12 Canadian yards engaged in this cargo boat programme have every reason to be proud of their contribution to the war effort. Recently the Burrard Dry Dock Company set a record by delivering the Fort Wedderbume in 89 days from the laying of the keel. At West Coast Ship Builders a ship has been launched forty-five days after the laying of the keel.
Our cargo shipbuilding programme is now at its peak. It will be maintained there. The entire programme is administered by Wartime Merchant Shipping Limited, one of the largest of our crown companies.
Practically all the shipbuilding at present being carried on by the united nations is designed to meet immediate war requirements. For this purpose the British shipping authorities developed a type of cargo ship known as the North Sands. This type was chosen because the components were suited to mass production by engineering shops and foundries not heretofore accustomed to serving shipbuilding, and the ship itself is suitable for construction in all types of shipyards, including new shipyards built and equipped hurriedly. The engine and boilers are of rugged construction, simplified for operation by a person of limited experience and easy to repair and maintain in all ports of the world.
The ship is suitable for carrying all types of cargo; general merchandise, crated motor vehicles, bulk grains, coal, ore, lumber, or munitions of all types, ranging up to the heaviest of guns and tanks.
This type, under the name of the Liberty ship, was also adopted by the United States Maritime Commission for their greatly expanded cargo shipbuilding programme; modified somewhat to suit their mass production methods. It constitutes an overwhelming proportion of the present vast American monthly ship output.
It should be clearly understood that the ship built in the United Kingdom and Canada under the name of North Sands ship is from the standpoint of hull design and horsepower exactly the same ship as is built in the United States under the name of Liberty ship. Consequently the rated speed of the

American Liberty and the Canadian and British North Sands is exactly the same, namely 11 knots. Our Canadian ships have exceeded 14 knots on their trials, without load, in smooth water and have averaged a speed of over 11 knots on a return voyage loaded between British Columbia and New Zealand.
This ship under service conditions is up to convoy speed. Increasing its speed would involve increasing the power plant by the cube of the increase in speed. To drive this ship at 11 knots requires 2,500 horse-power to drive it at 18 knots would require over 11,000 horse-power, in addition to which the ship itself must be redesigned. Any effective increase in speed gained by such a proportionately tremendous increase in power would involve building and tooling new plants for components manufacture, which could only be done after high expenditure and great delay. During the period of change-over less ship tonnage would be produced, at a time when ships of the type now being built are most urgently needed for war purposes. From the Canadian standpoint the building of faster ships is a post-war rather than a present-day war problem, for which the necessary advice is now being secured from the best sources.
A certain number of the North Sands type of ship were built as oil burners, with certain changes in design and equipment of a strictly operational nature. These have been named Victory ships, both here and in the United States.
Based upon our experience ini building the North Sands ships and the Victory ships, the necessary arrangements, are now being made to build next year an improved design of cargo ship to be known as the Modified North Sands ship, one of the characteristics of which will be its adaptability for either coal or fuel oil, which, under war or post-war conditions, will give the ship much greater operating flexibility.
Canadian export trade in peace-time consists chiefly of bulk cargoes of agricultural, forest, or mineral products. The 11-knot ship now being built will carry these cargoes at a lower ton mile cost than any faster ship which would necessarily cost much more to build, operate and maintain.
We are also building a limited number of 4,700-ton ships, of a design adopted by the British authorities for general and bulk cargo carrying to ports where the volume of trade is not large and the water is more shallow. These ships, which were originally designed for British operation, are now being modified to meet Canadian operating conditions. They are most suitable for Canadian coastwise trade and also to supply Labrador, Newfoundland and the West Indies.

During May, we launched a total of 17 escort craft.
In addition to the steel vessel programme, we have placed orders for 178 wooden patrol ships and wooden minesweepers. Of these, 100 were in the water by the end of May.

Air Services Branch (Department of Transport). The air services branch, comprising the civil aviation division, the meteorological division and the radio division, is responsible for the construction of all aerodromes and ancillary services in Canada, Newfoundland and Labrador which are required for home defence and for the British commonwealth air training plan. To date, the branch has spent over $100,000,000 on 286 projects, including the construction of 146 new aerodromes and extensive improvements to 51 others. In carrying out these projects, we have established some remarkable construction records thanks to the efficiency and enterprise of the Canadian construction industry which has displayed characteristic ingenuity in coping with difficult problems of climate and terrain.
The establishment of a very extensive network of operational and training fields has required a corresponding increase in meteorological and radio services. In addition to weather forecasting for Our passenger airway services, the meteorological division is providing the weather data for the R.A.F. ferry service across the Atlantic and the T.C.A. service between Canada and Newfoundland. It is also forecasting for the R.C.A.F. and naval units operating off the Atlantic and Newfoundland coasts, as well as the air .patrols on the Pacific coast north to the Alaska boundary. These responsibilities have meant a considerable increase in personnel in operating centres and the construction of new weather observation stations in many remote and isolated locations. We are now setting up radiosonde stations in various parts of the country for the purpose of recording weather conditions in the stratosphere for long range forecasting.
Since the outbreak of war 14 radio range and communication stations have been built and equipped by the radio division for the Department of National Defence for Air. Seven radio stations are nearing completion 
and we are planning the construction of 16 additional stations in the current year. The radio division is also collaborating closely with the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. Radio stations of the division along the east and west coasts and Hudson bay and Hudson strait and in the Canadian Arctic are now serving the navy. These stations form an important link in the aircraft detection programme and are, of course, of great value to the naval authorities in facilitating ship movements.
We have been successful in coordinating the Canadian radio services with the United States services, so that we are approaching the time when one single system of radio aids to navigation in the air and on the sea will service the north American continent.

Wartime Industries Control Board. The appointment of controllers to increase and conserve supplies of strategic materials has been subject to some criticism in this house and elsewhere. It is claimed that the system violates the principle of ministerial responsibility. I think I should tell the house that controllers are subject to the direction of the minister in all that they do. Their orders are issued with his full knowledge and concurrence. If we had not taken immediate steps to increase and conserve our supplies of strategic materials through curtailment, rationing and other means, it is quite certain that we should not have achieved the record of production which I have just outlined. The only possible alternative to curtailment and rationing was to take what we needed for war and essential industries, and let the public scramble for the rest. If we had followed this procedure, I am quite sure that we would now be criticized for not having taken steps to ensure the orderly distribution of materials which were in short supply. Admittedly, curtailment and rationing measures always contain an element of experiment. Inequities in distribution can only be discovered through trial. Where we have found such inequities, we have taken the necessary corrective steps. At the present time I believe our various curtailment and rationing programmes are accomplishing the main objective-the allocation of materials where they are needed most- with a minimum of hardship to the public.
Coal. Coal is one of our most pressing supply problems. Consumption has increased by more than 45 per cent since the war began. In 1939 we used 28,500,000 short tons; last year 41,500,000 short tons, and in the current year we expect to use 47,250,000 short tons. Since the 1938-1939 coal year Canadian production has increased, but to an extent much smaller than the proportionate increase in total consumption. The result is that we have relied to an increasing extent on imports from the United States. Since the war began our imports from the United States have nearly doubled. As requirements in the United States are also increasing, it is impossible to forecast with any degree of certainty what quantity of coal we can import from the United States in the current year. So far this year our United States imports have been lower by more than half a million tons than those of last year. All of this means that Canada faces a possible shortage of 4,000,000 short tons during the current year. We can

per year. We are using over half a million tons of steel per year to make tanks and other army vehicles.
Steel foundry capacity also has been expanded. The output of castings has risen from 61,000 tons in 1939 to 160,000 tons in 1942. These castings are used in a great variety of munitions from huge stern frames for cargo ships to parts for small arms.

Non-ferrous metals. Canada is the greatest base metal exporting country in the world, and this year our output will attain the highest peak in our history. This has been achieved by the enormous expansion of the aluminum industry, the development of a Canadian process for the production of magnesium, the extension of recovery operations at large base metal mines, the revival of old mines, the expansion of existing properties and the development and exploitation of new marginal and submarginal deposits.
The aluminum industry in Canada provides possibly our most spectacular story of wartime expansion. The Canadian output is more than six times that of 1939, is now greater than the total 1939 production of the rest of the world, and is supplying about 40 per cent of the war requirements of the United Nations.
Yet the demands are now so great-18,000 pounds are required for one large bomber- that civilian curtailments will continue until the war is over.
In the case of copper, nickel, lead and zinc the aggregate refined production is estimated at 827,800 tons for 1943, as against 662,100 tons in 1939.
Canada is now producing 95 per cent of the combined nickel output of the United Nations; 20 per cent of the zinc output; 124 per cent of the copper output; 15 per cent of the lead output; 75 per cent of the asbestos output; and 20 per cent of the mercury output. 
Formerly entirely dependent on imports for our supply of magnesium, we now have a government owned and operated magnesium plant, using a process developed in Canada, which supplies our own needs plus a surplus for export.
At the beginning of the war, we were lacking in such essential metals as tin, tungsten, motybdenum, mercury, chrome and manganese. Under the direction of a government company, Wartime Metals Corporation, every effort has been made to stimulate the production of these metals, and where necessary to build uip stock piles of imported metals. These efforts have met with a large measure of success.
We have discovered what appears to be one of the most important discoveries of tungsten on this continent. In the latter half of 1943 Canada should be well on the way to self-sufficiency in tungsten.
The search for molybdenum has met with considerable success. Two new properties, one financed by the government, wild be in operation in the latter half of this year, and their combined output should provide the major part of our requirements.
The development of mercury has been outstanding. Prior to the war, we were entirely dependent on imported supplies, but to-day Canada is one of the important producing countries of the world and we are exporting in quantity.
Chemicals. Although Canadian production has risen to unprecedented' heights, the supply of basic chemicals, such as alcohol, chlorine, glycerine, soda ash, and sulphuric acid, would be insufficient, if their uses were not constantly watched and, wherever necessary restricted.

I remind you that priorities on imported United States equipment are fixed by the priorities officers of the United States government, although application must be made through the Canadian priorities office.
Ship Repairs. Control of ship repairs and salvage is becoming increasingly important as the battle of the Atlantic reaches its peak. In the first three years of the war, apart from naval ships, Canada repaired 5,000 vessels averaging 4,000 gross tons each.
Now that Canada has assumed greater responsibilities in convoying ships to Britain, our activities in this field will continue to expand.
Since the salvage control was established in May, 1942, effective measures have been taken to recover ships and cargoes abandoned by owners or underwriters, and much valuable material has been salvaged.
Construction. Thousands of tons of valuable raw materials have been conserved for war and essential use by construction control. A restrictive order has placed all construction projects on a licence basis.
Many hundreds of projects have been postponed until after the war, and thus a backlog of post-war activity is being built up.
It is recognized that in crowded areas private dwellings must be built. In the last four months 5,622 licences for home construction have been issued.
Power. Our great resources of electrical power provide one of the basic reasons why Canada now holds fourth place among the united nations as a war producer. The unfavourable winter season and the lateness of the ice break-up this year severely tested our power facilities.
With still more power plants and facilities going into operation this year, it would now seem safe to assume that, if present restrictions are maintained, we need have no fear for the future.
It took Canada forty-five years to bring power installations up to 7,155,000 horse-power in 1938. In the short time since war began, new developments, including the enormous Shipshaw undertaking and certain other projects not yet completed, will have added an effective electrical capacity of 1,870,000 horsepower.
Since the beginning of the war, interconnections between power systems have been made more elastic and of great capacity. Power has been loaned from time to time between the United States and Canada. In times of break-down, power has been transmitted to the United States at Niagara, and taken from the United States at Beauharnois, or vice versa, depending on the needs of the moment. In all respects the relations between the Canadian and American controls have been cooperative and helpful.
In Ontario, production has been materially increased by the completion of the Big Eddy development, the Madawaska development, and the submerged weir in the Niagara river. The DeCew Falls development is nearing completion. In Quebec, all the power companies have greatly increased their output, and the Shipshaw development alone has increased the installations this year by 600,000 horse-power. Additional generators are being installed monthly. In Alberta, the Minnewanka de-. velopment has been completed; and in British Columbia, the Brilliant development is proceeding. In all the provinces, improved storage facilities, together with the installation of new machinery, have made more power available. All this new power must be used for war and essential purposes.
The gas situation in southwestern Ontario has been improved by additional drilling and by completion of a part of the new coke-oven gas plant at Hamilton. Of necessity, the gas restrictions have been very severe on many families in that area. It is hoped that when the new ovens at Hamilton are completed. and with full use of the still gas at Sarnia, all requirements for war production will be met, and some cases of individual hardship may be mitigated.
Motor Vehicle Control. Only a limited number of new trucks are being released and such releases are only for the most vital purposes. It follows, therefore, that owners of existing trucks are the custodians of irreplaceable property of importance in the war programme, and, as such, they must take every precaution to keep their trucks in good running order. Every assistance is being given to operators and garagemen to assure adequate essential repair facilities.
.3556
War Appropriation-Supplies

The transfer of used trucks from essential industries, such as farming, mining, lumbering and general haulage, is causing serious difficulties, and is likely to become critical during the harvesting of the western crops. This problem is receiving careful consideration.
Transit. With drastic restrictions on gasoline and tires for private vehicles, the public transit systems have been faced with the almost impossible task of handling approximately twice as much traffic as before the war with few additional vehicles.
In some eleven centres all across Canada the hours of approximately 351,500 office, factory, and store employees, including 39,000 government employees in Ottawa, have been staggered to relieve peak pressure on transit facilities.
, When gasoline rationing became necessary, a need developed to utilize private passenger cars to transport workers in essential industries. Many of our war plants are not adequately served by car and bus lines. Late last year there was put into operation the wartime industrial transit plan which permits in certain approved plants the choice of a sufficient number of employee owner-drivers whose responsibility it is to provide the transportation needs of their fellow workers. In return these owner-drivers are the only employees of the plants entitled to special gasoline and tire privileges. By the end of April 1943, the plan was in operation in more than 1,500 plants and industries in Canada. 48,000 cars transport approximately 195,000 workmen, and as a result approximately 38,000 special gasoline categories have been eliminated.
Urban bus mileage curtailment now results in a saving of 4,687,000 bus miles per annum. Inter-urban bus mileage curtailment now effects a saving of 21,700,000 bus miles per annum. This is a net saving. A gross saving which includes mileage diverted to the exclusive transportation of war workers and armed forces would be considerably larger. Further savings are anticipated on summer schedules. Restrictions on the operation of taxicabs have also produced considerable saving in gasoline and rubber.
Transport. Handicapped by increasingly serious shortages of rolling stock and1 personnel, the railroads of this country have had to contend with very serious operating problems.
Restrictions such as the curtailment of extra sections, the elimination of special trains, the cancellation of special fares, including week-end rates, and the provision, to as great an extent as possible, for maximum
1 Mr. Howe.]
loading of freight cars, have resulted in substantial reductions in the use of railway equipment, and substantial increases in the movement of freight.
The railways of Canada are doing a magnificent job. Despite the handicap of less personnel and equipment, they are now handling 50 per cent more traffic than ever before in their history.
I have endeavoured to give hon. members a brief summary of the work of the Department of Munitions and Supply and to indicate the present state of war production. The day to day problems in this field do not lessen. Shortages of man-power have developed, particularly in coal mining, base metal mining, forest industries, in common labour for steel mills and allied industries, and for construction work, and are being dealt with effectively by selective service. It must not be forgotten that more than 700,000 of our younger men, all physically fit, are in the armed services, and that their loss to industry has made necessary widespread readjustments of our remaining man-power.
A recent check of our production personnel indicates that only about 4 per cent of the men in industry were on deferment from military services as of March 1 last. The percentage of deferments in industiy has been considerably reduced since then. This should disprove conclusively the statement frequently made that war industry is in competition with the armed services for men. It is quite proper at this stage of our production programme that the armed services should have complete precedence within the age group that have been called up for military service. It is our policy that deferments are asked only for men having specialized training and skill of a type that is absolutely essential to our programme. Women are playing an ever increasing part in war production and there has been no loss of efficiency on that account. Lost time as a result of labour disputes has been trivial, when compared with the record of any allied country. The output of war material from Canadian factories is a fine tribute to the loyalty and devotion of the men and women employed in our many war plants and war industries. When the history of Canada's participation in the war is written, those men and women will deserve to share with our armed services a full measure of recognition.
Canadian industry has developed remarkably under the stimulus of war. Never again will there be any doubt that Canada can manufacture anything that can be manufactured elsewhere. Our industry has pioneered production

War Appropriation-Naval Services
in many new lines of war material, and has brought about improvements in many older manufacturing processes. Its equipment has been modernized, and its productive capacity has been expanded out of all comparison with our pre-war industry.
Later in this debate my associate, the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier), will report on cost reductions that have been effected in our war plants.
I would like to mention especially the devotion to duty of the officers of my department, many of whom are serving without salary. I have drafted into the service of the department the men whom I consider best qualified by experience to direct its varied activities. Among them are many who came to the department with established reputations in the field of production. I am sure that industry will agree with me that their expert direction has had no small part in bringing our war programme to its present effectiveness.
The production programme of Canada has been meshed in with that of the United Kingdom, United States and other allied countries through Canadian membership on the combined production and resources board and through close contact with all allied production agencies. The Department of Munitions and Supply has branch offices in Washington and in London, England, with organizations duplicating in skeleton form our organization here in Ottawa. I feel that ours is a department of government capable of meeting the many and varied problems involved in a manufacturing and supply programme that is straining Canada's capacity to the utmost. However long the war may be, I am confident that there will be no break in Canada's production front. Therefore, I do not hesitate to ask hon. members to approve the appropriations now under consideration.

speechtext: I do not think any waters have been designated as a theatre of war in the sense of the order in council, but any men serving on a Canadian ship of war in any of our coastal waters would be on active service and would automatically be pensionable. speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
That is quite correct. The insurance principle applies to those outside Canada in the air or in the navy, or with the land troops, and disability or death incurred during such service is pensionable. For those who have served only in Canada, death or disability is pensionable if it arises out of service or is attributable to service. The insurance principle does

We are beginning to do a good deal of printing both for ourselves and for the British admiralty, in the way of confidential books and that sort of thing, and I think it is a good arrangement for both of us. I am not sure about the manuals of seamanship; there may have been a considerable store of those on hand in Great Britain, and they may be still available.
Is the money for teletypes for purchase or rental?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: For rental.
To whom is the rental paid?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Generally to the communications companies. There are teletypes running from here to Washington, from here to Halifax and to St. John's, Newfoundland; and I think we have another one to London, England.
A direct one to England?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, I think we have, at this moment. We have them to various places throughout the country. Rentals are paid to the cable, telegraph and telephone companies.
In connection with the matters contained in this item, was the minister's department under the jurisdiction of the director of economies control, about which we have heard something this session.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes, I think so. I have never been sure, but 1 think I was.
And how did the minister get along -with him?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not think I had much occasion to apply to the director of economies control. I believe I did make application to him, but it was in connection with a matter which really did not require an application. He was pleased to grant the request. I think I had occasion only once to write to him.

Just a little pleasant formality.

War Appropriation-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes; to show there was good feeling between us.

Recently and since the beginning of the war we have read in the papers about the hardships suffered by survivors from torpedoed ships, and the difficulties they have in feeding themselves. I understand that in the United States rafts and boats are now fitted' up with light fishing tackle. Has this department done the same thing?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes; we have a complete kit for life-saving. As I said the other night, it includes concentrated food, such as chocolate, and that sort of thing. Then I believe a fishing line and, some hooks are included in the kit.
It would be very light, and would not require much space.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It would not take much space.
There was an article in this morning's newspaper about a new suit invented by a Canadian.
A zoot suit.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The navy is very much against the zoot variety.

The article states that the suit was invented by a Canadian in Toronto. It is equipped with considerable apparatus, and packed with kapok, to keep afloat those who may fall into the water. Among other things it is equipped with a flashlight attached to the top of the cap, and this light flashes on and off. The article states the authorities are purchasing quite a number of these suits. Is a number being purchased by the minister's department, and, if so, under what item?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Various designs of life-saving suits are constantly before the department. I am not aware that we have actually made any agreement with the gentleman from Toronto for the purchase of the suit about which the hon. member speaks. I know that a year or two ago, Mr. Gordon Leitch of Toronto was interested in a certain kind of suit which he felt would be helpful to shipwrecked men. From time to time various designs of belts, clothing and pullovers which will help to keep a man afloat have been submitted. I am not sure, however, that we have made any definite commitments for the suit mentioned by the 'hon. member.

The flashlight is in the
cap, and operates on and off. When the man
falls or is thrown into the water from a ship he pulls the cap over his head and the light goes on and off, like a lighthouse light.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes;
I know about it.

Dehydrated rations were
a Canadian invention, were they not? Has this ration been adopted by the Royal Navy, andl, if so, with what results? Has it been as successful as we hoped?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
In
one form or another life-boat rations have been tried out by various countries. Great Britain had a life-boat ration. Our men studied' it, and made some changes in it. They were very successful in providing water and food Which would not go stale. I know that the ration designed here by our naval medical research unit attracted much attention in Great Britain andl the United States. I am not in a position to say whether they have actually adopted it, but I know they were keenly interested and asked for samples, which we were glad to send them.

The British navy have
adopted our dehydrated' food on all ships?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

Doctor Best of
Toronto deserves great credit for the fine work he has done in connection with perfecting life-boat rations. He has been living on submarines and on ships, under the most trying conditions, and I am happy to pay him tribute for all he has done in this connection.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
agree, entirely. His work has been of a very high order.
I understood the minister to say that $258,000 was spent on code books. Are those books manufactured in Canada? Are they purchased from firms in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They are not purchased from firms. They are being printed by the naval department, itself, in Ottawa.
What does the laundry item include? Does the navy launder sailors' uniforms?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I
think this laundry item includes sheets, pillowcases, blankets, hospital bedding and supplies of that kind. I do not think it includes the personal laundry of officers or men.

Do sailors have to look after their own uniforms? How about the white uniforms?

This is an omnibus item, and offers me an opportunity to bring a matter to the attention of the minister. All of us agree as to the wonderful development which has taken place in the Canadian navy. However, there is always room for improvement, and one matter has been brought to my attention by a number of naval officers. I refer to giving greater consideration to officers of the R.C.N.V.R. in the matter of promotions, and the like.
Is it a fact that there is any difference between pay received by officers of the R.C.N. and those of the R.C.N.V.R.? My further argument will be based upon the minister's answer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is no difference in the pay of R.C.N. and R.C.N.V.R. officers of the same ranks.
Is there any difference in the allowances?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No.

I am advancing the argument I intend to advance not by way of criticism but in an effort to secure information on this subject and thus be able to reassure these RC.N.V.R. officers who represent about eighty to eighty-five per cent of the men in the navy. They feel that they are deserving of greater representation on the naval board than they have had heretofore. Has the minister given consideration to increasing this representation? Is there any representative of the R.C.N.V.R, on the naval board?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The secretary of the board is an R.C.N.V.R. officer.
That is Captain Pennington.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.
Is it expected that he will shortly leave the board?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If he does, I should think we would probably replace him with another R.C.N.V;R. officer.
How many members are there of the naval board? Is there only the one man representing the R.C.N.V.R., who make up about eighty-five per cent of the personnel of the navy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The naval board consists of the chief of naval staff, the vice-chief of naval staff, the chief of naval engineering, the chief of naval equipment and supply, the chief of naval personnel, the deputy minister, the secretary, and I sit in with the board myself. My hon. friend will understand that the board is made up of the senior officers of the department, the heads of branches and that sort of thing, and it is not always possible perhaps to get a R.C.N.V.R. officer who has had the necessary training, and experience to fit him tc be the head of a department. There are some departments that R:C.N.V.R. officers could head very well.
What departments would they be?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That would depend upon the experience of the particular officer. It is obvious that the chief of naval staff would be expected to be a permanent officer, and I think that would apply also to the vice-chief of naval staff who must take the place of the chief in his absence. The chief of naval engineering and construction, Admiral Stephens, is an engineering officer of something like thirty-five years' experience, and it would be quite difficult to find a R.C.N.V.R. officer with the necessary naval engineering experience. Many of them are qualified engineers, but ' they have not had the naval experience that Admiral Stephens has had. Personnel might be a place where a R.C.N.V.R. officer of the right type could perform satisfactory work.
If that were done, I think it would remove a lot of the reason for complaint.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The secretary of the naval board is a R.C.N.V.R. officer. The deputy minister is a civilian, and if there is such a thing as a civilian viewpoint, he would have it. I must say that I have not heard of the complaints to which my hon. friend referred, but I might not hear of them. A lot of the R.C.N.V.R. officers who come back from the sea to Ottawa call in to see me and they talk quite frankly. I always encourage them to do that, but I must say that I have not heard of these complaints. I should be very sorry to think there was any feeling: between the three branches of the navy. In this regard we follow the Royal Navy's system which has the same three branches. Our navy is only about thirty years old; it is Obvious that we should have some model and guide,, and I do not know where we could get a better model and guide than the British navy' itself.

War Appropriation-Naval Services

Has any consideration been given to appointing a R.C.N.Y.R. officer as personnel representative on the naval board? The navy is the only service in Canada where any distinction is made between officers who served prior to the war and those who have volunteered since. I am placing this matter before the minister in all sincerity. He says that none of these complaints has come to him, but I can understand that. If the naval regulations are similar to the army regulations, an officer would have no right to make a complaint except through the regular channels.
In making the suggestion that there should be a greater representation of the R.C.N.V.R. on the naval board, I do so out of consideration for the wishes of a number of these officers who have spoken to me. In the course of conversation with at least ten of them the same matter was raised. The minister says that the secretary of the board is a R.C.N.V.R. officer, but ordinarily secretaries have little to say. We all want to see the navy built up; we all want to see it achieve greater efficiency and cbntinue the magnificent work it has been doing; but if there is any ground for the complaint made by these R.C.N.V.R. officers that they are not receiving fair and proper representation on the board, that their ideas do not receive the proper attention, the minister should give it attention. If this is done, I feel that there will be great dividends in the way of morale, and it certainly would do no harm in connection with policy. The majority of those on the board would be permanent officers, but at the same time there would be brought into the discussions of the naval staff the viewpoint of those who had been civilians previously. The civilian viewpoint, the viewpoint of the man who has entered the service since the outbreak of the war, would be refreshing and might do a great deal to improve conditions which in many instances are not known as well by those who make a profession of the service.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for what he has said. He has made a constructive and helpful suggestion. I shall bear it very carefully and very fully in mind. I might say that in all those branches which are headed by members of the permanent service of the Royal Canadian Navy, there are a great many Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve men serving. A goodly number of the officers serving with the head of the naval personnel branch would be R.C.N.V.R. officers; and in that way their views, I should think, would become well known to the head of the branch.
As I said, however, I shall be glad to consider the whole matter with the utmost care, and once more I thank my hon. friend for what he has said and the spirit in which he has said it.

Last evening I asked the minister what was the tonnage of the corvettes, Fairmiles, and some of the other ships in the navy. The minister said he did not know whether he should answer that question, and I did not press it. I ask him now if he would be prepared to tell us what is the tonnage of the smallest class of ship in the Canadian navy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I mentioned, I think several times, that we had fighting ships, and ships which, while very useful, were not of that type. Does my hon. friend mean the smallest vessel of any sort that we have, or is he referring to combat ships?
What I really had in mind was the fighting ships in the 550.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I fancy the smallest of the 550 would be some of the armed yachts. Some of these are larger than Fairmiles; there may be some which are smaller. I am not exactly sure whether our smallest fighting ship is the armed yacht or the Fail-mile. I would have to look over the tonnage of all the armed yachts and compare them with the Fairmile tonnage in order to answer that.

The item of sundries includes, as is natural, a great many small items. council for scientific services, $539,000; unemployment insurance stamps, $95,000; temporary civil servants, $54,000, which is for the unemployment insurance scheme; casual labour, $33,000 at Halifax and $7,000 at Esquimalt; bonding premiums, $3,000 to pay for bonds held on naval personnel who handle public funds; administration of merchant seamen's order, $46,000; rehabilitation grants, $141,000; small grants for Prince Robert house on the west coast, a hostel there,, $1,200; pension to ex-skipper White, $363; unforeseen expenses, $568,000; contingencies, $130,000,
Is that $1,200 the total contribution of the government to Prince Robert house?

Would the minister explain just what happens to a suggested invention that is sent in to the department? What exactly is done with it? Is there an inventions board or an inventions branch in connection with his department, or does the national research council deal entirely with it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We have a man to whom such matters are frequently referred. There is also an inventions board which is attached to the national research council, and they are the people who pass on a great many of these inventions.
At some stage the navy must give its opinion on that, and I wondered whether it gave its opinion before the invention went to the national research council or at a later stage.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I report progress?

Before the estimate
finally goes through, this seemed to me to be an appropriate occasion, at the conclusion of the consideration of the estimates of the three defence departments under the war appropriation bill resolution, for the members of this house to pause and to reflect for a moment upon the giant contribution which the officers and non-commissioned officers and the men and women of all three branches of our armed forces are making in a cause for which this nation and empire in collaboration with the other united nations are fighting, for the preservation of a free, democratic way of life.

Well over a month has been consumed in the consideration of the appropriations which will enable our forces to continue to make that contribution. During the debate there has been active and constructive criticism by members of this house. On mafly occasions there has been disagreement both as to policy and as to detail. On several occasions this disagreement has reached a high pitch. I rather think, for instance, that the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services will, upon reflection, agree that one of the most dangerous and perhaps one of the most delicate positions in which he found himself during the consideration of his estimates was when he singled out for special mention the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church); for this member's name may properly be said to be synonymous with the armed forces and their dependents for whom he has worked indefatig-ably for well over a quarter of a century.
However, we of the Progressive Conservative party have only attempted to meet the government in debating collision where we felt that the government in the interests of the nation and particularly in the interests of the armed forces, required that type of criticism in order that it may itself be rendered more capable, more competent and more efficient to do the services which the people of Canada desire it at this time to do.
There is something about'democracy, however, which must not be overlooked. Right in this chamber are the representatives of the people who, while differing as to policy, method and detail in many instances, will rise up in one concordant unit, one member vying with another, on the one and only important issue facing Canada to-day, namely, the bringing of the present hostilities to a victorious conclusion.
We as civilians in Canada during this wartime period try to do our best, but that best falls far short of our armed forces' best. The achievements of the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force have aroused in Canadians an enthusiastic, justifiable pride in' the heroism and the valour of the men and the officers of all three services.
I think, therefore, that this parliament should at this moment put aside all its petty cleavages, all its little thoughts, and concentrate upon tendering our appreciation to those hundreds of thousands of our men and women who are prepared to lay upon the altar of sacrifice, if needs be, all that they have, including that dearest of all treasures, life itself. To them in the midst of [DOT] our deilberations with respect to the financial requirements needed to support them, I desire to place upon the record of parliament, not

Supply-The late Hon. W. R. Motherwell
only on behalf of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition but on behalf of the entire membership of this House of Commons, a tribute of grateful recognition of their high position in our thoughts and in our minds to-day.
We solemnly recall and remember the sacrifice made by those who have fallen in this war; and to those of their kin upon whom their loss falls most heavily, we express our heartfelt and genuine sympathy at this time.
This can be little more than a gesture of this house, but we who are not privileged to serve in the more dangerous fields of conflict, at least owe it to those who do, to display to them this unity of thought and purpose, which goes much more deeply than any inadequate words of mine can properly express.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since I was last before the committee with my estimates I was called upon to attend the funeral of the late Hon. W. R. Motherwell, who had preceded me as Minister of Agriculture. The fact that during the almost eight years that I have had the privilege of being Minister of Agriculture four men have passed away who had

3568	COMMONS
Supply-The late Hon. W. R. Motherwell
formerly occupied this position in earlier days, suggests to us the rate at which time passes. No life could have exemplified more completely the importance of making full use of the time that is allotted than the life of Hon. W. R. Motherwell. He was given thirteen years longer than the allotted span, and during the whole period of his life has been busily engaged in doing those things which he considered to be in the interests of agriculture.
He was born a few miles from this city, in Lanark county. He won a scholarship which took him early in life to the Guelph agricultural college, where he graduated with honours as one of its first class. Shortly after graduation he journeyed west to locate as a practical farmer on a piece of raw prairie which, in a period of about twenty years, he converted into one of the finest farm homes in Canada. He made the trip west from the end of steel by ox-cart and turned his first sod with oxen, but he lived to see the farm equipped with the most up-to-date machinery and farmed by the most modern and most up-to-date methods. Mr. Motherwell accomplished the difficult task of remaining a practical dirt farmer while keeping up to date as a technical agriculturist. This part of the story comes to me second hand, but the remainder of his life was so closely intermingled with my own that his passing has removed a faithful friend and a helpful adviser.
In 1904 I went to what is now Saskatchewan. My first political experience was in assisting to elect the first government of Saskatchewan, in which Mr. Motherwell was minister of agriculture, in 1905. In 1911 I became principal of a school in his home constituency and in 1914 entered the legislature as his representative, supporting the government of which he was a member. In 1921 he became my representative in the House of Commons for the federal constituency of Melville, and in 1940 I became his representative in the House of Commons for the federal constituency of Melville. For thirty-two years we lived within sight of each other's home. I therefore speak of him to-night as a close neighbour, as a long-time political friend and as my most valued tutor in matters pertaining to agriculture. He was a man with whom one could feel honoured to be in agreement and with whom one hesitated to be in disagreement because of his wide experience, great knowledge, unquestioned integrity and his conscientious pursuit of his convictions.
Mr. Motherwell's service to agriculture is written into the records of farm organizations, first in the province of Saskatchewan, later

across Canada and, -while Minister of Agriculture of Canada, across the world. His great energy and organizing ability found expression in the territorial and iSaskatehewan grain growers' associations, which laid the community foundation for every cooperative farm organization in western Canada. During his period as minister in Saskatchewan he laid the legislative base for every cooperative farm organization in that province, and brought arts, science, engineering, law', medical and agricultural students together on one campus. During his service in Ottawa he promoted cooperatives, encouraged the grading of farm products and fought in a practical way every parasite and disease which attacked animal and plant life, crowning 'his efforts by organizing an attack upon rust in wheat. His outstanding international achievements were those of arranging to have the world poultry and wheat conferences held in Canada.
His long and useful service in agriculture was acknowledged by his friends while he still lived, in two ways: first, by hanging a life-size portrait of himself in the agricultural college he established at Saskatoon, and second, by gathering in his long cherished Qu'Appelle valley, the beauty spot of the prairie west, to present him with a substantial purse and express their appreciation of his services. But his greatest joy came from the fact that his only grandson, who had reached the age of maturity and who graduated with the highest honours from the institution Mr. Motherwell had established at Saskatoon, did him the honour just before his death of taking over the old homestead, thus keeping in the name of its creator the farm which has meant so much to Canada.
I was gratified to have the privilege of representing the government of Canada and you, the agriculture committee, before which he stood so often, at the graveside of a matchless farmer, a technical and practical agriculturist, a Canadian statesman whose name will live in the annals of western Canadian pioneering life. It was my privilege to carry to his widow, his son, his daughter, his grandson and granddaughter, all of whom are highly honoured in their own right by all who know them, your sympathy and your appreciation of a life well lived. At the same time I should like to say to this committee that I believe the passing of Mr. Motherwell marks the end of an era in the development of agricultural life in the great central section of Canada. He was one of the pioneers. In his death we witnessed the

Supply-The late Hon. W. R. Motherwell
passing of one who did much to make possible the settlement of people in the western part of this country and to make of Canada a greater country.
While I was west I had the opportunity of attending the funeral of a neighbour of Mr. Motherwell, whose life marks, I think, the beginning of a new era, not only in the agriculture of the west but in the experiences of Canada as a nation. This man, Doctor Hiel, had not reached an age at which we expect men to pass on. He was a young man, only thirty-three years of age. Into his life, however, he had crowded more than most of us are able to crowd into a span of seventy or eighty years. He was the youngest person ever to graduate from the university of Saskatchewan, entering that university before he was fifteen and graduating in due course. He took a course in medicine at the university of Toronto and passed with honours. He spent a year as an interne at the sanatorium in the province of Saskatchewan, a year as an interne at the Civic hospital in Ottawa, a year as an interne at the Bedford hospital in Great Britain, and took a post-graduate course in Vienna. Then he spent a year as surgeon on a British ship sailing out of Liverpool. Two years before the war he came home and began to practise medicine in Timmins, Ontario. When the war started he enlisted, and two weeks ago passed away in a hospital in Toronto, following an attack of pneumonia. He was brought to his old farm home to be buried, in the same neighbourhood in which Mr. Motherwell had lived.
As a comment on the statements made the other evening by the hon. member for Vegre-ville I should like to describe to this committee what I experienced at that funeral. This young man was one of a family of ten; he was the fourth boy of a group of seven, all born and raised on a farm in Saskatchewan; On this occasion he was dressed in the uniform of a captain of His Majesty's forces; over the coffin in which he was placed was draped the union jack, and the coffin was carried by his six brothers. Of those six brothers the first two were in uniform; one was a lieutenant in the army, serving on the Pacific coast and the other was a private in the army also serving on the Pacific coast. Of the two brothers immediately following, one had a teacher's degree, and had taught school in Saskatchewan, while the other had the degree of M.A., and is principal to-day of the high school grades in a school of which the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) was principal until a short time ago, and of which I had the privilege of being principal some 72537-2261
years previously. Behind those two were two other young men, one a farmer, farming in his own right, and the other a grain buyer who had farmed for a number of years and then taken up the position of grain buyer.
But a most important fact is that following these six young men were the father and mother. And that father and mother .were over seventy years of age. With them were two daughters, the third being in eastern Canada, the wife of a young man of foreign nationality who came east to take his part in making munitions, in order that this war might be prosecuted to a successful conclusion.
The point I wished to make particularly is that the mother and father came to this country from Europe. They were of German nationality, having come here from Austria before they were twenty years of age. They married in Canada, raised their family on a farm in western Canada, and made their living from the soil, soil which had never been broken before they broke it. They worked out of that soil the education of that family, consisting of the group of boys and girls I have described.
The further point I make is this: We were led ipto a church of the Lutheran faith. The service was conducted in the German language, and the hymns were sung in both German and English at the same time. A thousand people attended that service-Poles, Germans, Anglo-Saxons, and people of other nationalities. But I am sure hon. members in the committee will agree with me that an incident of that kind in a country such as ours, under these conditions, does mark the opening of a new era, an era of international understanding among all the nationalities who have come to this country, an understanding which will result and has already resulted in the building of a lasting Canadianism.
I recite these two incidents, one to mark the passing of the great pioneering age in western Canada, and the other to mark what has become a united feeling among our people in support of the institutions of government which make freedom possible in this country, and out of which true Canadianism will grow. The men we honour by mentioning them here were builders of a better and greater Canada.
