The boys in the army who are essential to agriculture will have to be sent home to the farm to stay there, and the only military training for them should be for the reserve army, the training to take place during the off seasons for agriculture.
Another thing that has been pointed out to me and, I am sure, to other hon. members, is that hired help is asking such tremendous wages that the farmers simply cannot pay them. The price the farmer receives for his products is not sufficient for him to pay the high wages that are being asked to-day. Ordinary farm labour this spring was asking for seven dollars a day. That was in threshing time this spring. With present prices the ' farmer simply cannot pay it. Then what is going to happen? Just what happened last year. The farmers are not going to pay such wages because their returns are not sufficient to enable them to do so; it is not because they do not want to do so. The result will be that this year there will be a great drop in the production of foodstuffs. If somebody suggests that instead of raising so much wheat the farmers should go into mixed farming because that does not require as much labour, he is definitely wrong. Anyone who has had to feed cattle during the winter would never make a suggestion of that kind.
We shall have to control the wages the farmers are asked to pay, or we shall have to increase the prices which the farmer receives for his products, so that he will be able to pay these high wages. I am not blaming the fellows who are out working for hire, because they see men who are working in industries in the cities getting high wages. Mind you, they do not work as long as the fellows who have to work on the farms. When you get up at five o'clock in the morning and work until ten o'clock at night you earn your $7, but when you work in an industry you do your eight hours and then go home. Of course some farmers are a little better off than others; they may have a little more power equipment, but there will have to be an adjustment in the prices of farm products. I do not think the bonus scheme is at all satisfactory. I believe the principle is wrong, when you give farmers bonuses for not raising wheat. I think if you

In addition to all that, there is the tremendous worry of how the mortgage is to be paid.
Let me give an illustration to-night. This man has been farming for about thirty-five years. He had a mortgage of $7,000 on his farm. Those of us who were on the war expenditures committee last year know definitely that wages do not concern the industrialist very much because they are all figured in the cost of production. I do not see what objection the other members of the cabinet could have if the Minister of Agriculture were to say: We are not asking any favours for agriculture; we want it placed on exactly the same footing as other essential industries. No logical, sane individual, even though he happens to be a cabinet minister, could possibly object to that. Is it not discrimination to the nth degree when we ask the farming people to pay double the wages they have been paying, yet say that they dare not add that increased cost to their cost of production, and that we will not compensate them in any way for it?
As a result of the labour condition that existed last year, farmers were not able to have their grain threshed, and in my district, owing to mice, they suffered a definite loss of ten bushels to the acre. Why? That was no fault of their own; it was partly due to the weather, but it was partly the fault of the Department of Labour, because the farmers did not have the help they needed. If an industry in this country is held back through no fault of its own, that extra cost is immediately added to the cost of production. We never ran across an industry in all of Canada that had to stand those losses, and moreover we did not run across one instance in all our travels across the country last year in which an industry was even asked to stand that loss. It was a foregone conclusion that all these added costs were to go into the cost of production, and then, in addition, industry is given what it considers a reasonable profit. Surely it is not asking too much to say that agriculture should be treated in exactly the same way. It is not a case of pleading for agriculture; it is a case of stating the facts, and hon. members of this house should demand of the government that this be done.

I wish to say a word
in regard to the farm labour situation. I come from a constituency in which the only industry is farming; there is no other industry at all, only the small villages which exist to meet the convenience of the farmers. While labour is not abundant in my constituency, still there is no labour shortage. The farmers all have their crop in again this year. It is true that last year we had a big crop and

we were not able to get it all harvested, but that was not on account of any shortage of help. There was plenty of help; people were walking the streets, unable to get any work, and that condition was owing to the weather. During the month of September we were able to work on the land for only four days; the rain prevented us from doing any harvesting. During the month of October we were able to use a combine for only eight days, and the result was that our crop was left on until this spring. But some weeks ago all our crop was in, and it is looking well; there 'has been plenty of rain.
I wish to say also that throughout my constituency there will be found very few boys remaining on the farms. They are practically all somewhere in the forces, in the army, the navy or the air force. The only boys left there now are not able to go into the forces on account of their physical condition. Most of our boys were volunteers, and I do not think it is fair or right for the hon. member for Bow River to say that these young men enlisted because they were afraid they might be conscripted. The boys in my constituency did not enlist for that reason; they enlisted of their own accord. They were not afraid of conscription or anything else. Many of them enlisted long before they became twenty-one years of age, when they might be conscripted. Many of those boys who volunteered have gone overseas, and they are there willingly, not because they were afraid of anything.
Farming conditions in western Canada are now quite different from what they were. When I went to western Canada and was farming in the district of Abernethy, wdien we would farm a half-section of land, 320 acres, we would put about 200 acres in crop and would summer-fallow 100 acres. In the spring of the year a man would have to hire another man to help him. He would get his crop in, and then summer-fallow his own 100 acres himself. When the fall came he would have to hire another man to do the stocking, and half a dozen or a dozen men would come in to help him take it off and thresh it.
To-day farming conditions in Ihe district I come from are the very opposite. We can now farm two and a half sections, 1,600 acres, with just as little farm help as was required on half a section some years ago, and we can do the farming in the same time. We take 1,600 acres to-day, and pay a man to work the combine. We seed 800 acres, and one man can do it all. When he hqs done the seeding he turns round, takes off the seeding attachment, uses the one-way and sumfner-

fallows the other 800 acres, keeping it black all summer. When the crop is ready to harvest, a man is hired to run the combine and another to drive the truck. They can take off a crop that required ten or twelve or fifteen men in earlier times.
To-day we do not have those big harvesting excursions coming from eastern Canada that we had years ago. Any who came into my district last year were not needed.
Why did you not get your crop harvested?

On account of the
weather. That is the same reason why many people in eastern Canada have not been able to put in their crops this year-the weather. If they were able to get to work on the land for six days, they would get their crops in. But where you can work for only one or two days in a week it is a different proposition. It is the same way with us. We had adverse weather conditions. If we had had more combines, then in the days we could work we would get more off. But men were no help to us. We wanted machinery. We want weather; and if we do not get the weather, and enough machines to take off the crop, then it cannot be taken off; that is all there is to it.
Cannot the government do anything about the weather?
Sometimes we think it should. It is nice to have the weather with us, anyway.
The hon. member might be a good minister of weather.

The hon. member for Bow River has referred to bonuses, and has said that the bonuses were not satisfactory. I want to say to him that I lived in a district where for ten years we had no crop, and almost ninety-nine per cent of the farmers were on relief. It was God's blessing when we got off relief and received the bonus.
You should have farm insurance, not a bonus.
We received the benefits of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which is a sort of insurance against crop failure.
What we should have is complete crop insurance.

That was one of the best pieces of legislation for the farmers of western Canada ever passed by this House of Commons. And I defy the hon. member, or anybody else, to go into my constituency and tell my people it was not.

I would be delighted to.
Come on and tell them, and see how you will be received.

I probably
will.

They believe it was the best piece of legislation ever put on the statute books as insurance against crop failure. A man does his work, puts in his crop; then Providence is against him, and he gets nothing. It is not his fault. . This is some sort of insurance against that very thing. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act does relieve the burden, a little. Nothing had a greater effect in undermining the morale of our people in western Canada than had relief. This is one method whereby the necessity for relief is lessened, and we are getting away from it.
A poor method.
It is for the poor man, or the rich man, or anybody else.
I said it was a poor method.

The big farmer suffers the same as anybody else. It is just as bad for him as it is for the other man.
Then the hon. member for Bow River mentioned a while ago that wages in industry had increased, but that farmers are not being treated in the same way. I suppose my hon. friend is a wheat grower, and he surely knows that in the last three or four months the price of wheat has gone up over ten per cent. Surely he knows that the price of wheat is now $1.01 or $1.02 a bushel, whereas not long ago it was only 90 cents. If that is not operating on behalf of the farmer, the same as it is for industry, I should like to know what it is.
Why has it gone up three cents in the last three days?

Some hon. members have been asking that the grain exchange be closed. What will they do when it comes to that? If the grain exchange had not been open we would not have known that the price was $1.01 or $1.02.
I do not intend to take up the time of the committee any further. I wish only to say this, that so far as farming conditions in western Canada are concerned this year, we still have plenty of help in the section of the country from which I come. We have our crop in, and we will take it off.

I had not intended to say anything about man-power, because I have said something about that already. But when the hon. member for Wood Mountain was talking about that one-way seeder attachment I was wondering how he was going to fill the bacon and dairy quotas. I happen to live in western Canada, and I am sorry to say that in my constituency we have a distinct labour shortage. We do operate more than the one-way and a combine, and I think that condition prevails throughout most of the area where diversified farming is practised. I know something about the conditions which prevail in my hon. friend's riding, and I think what he said is correct, so far as it applies to that part of the country. But that certainly does not prevail throughout western Canada. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture would not say he was satisfied with that kind of production.
I did not say that was the only thing we did.
The hon. member was not able to say much else, either.
My hon. friend might be surprised at what I might say.

I do not wish to repeat any argument that has been made, both at the last session and at this one, as to the condition agricultural producers face to-day. I am sure we expect a greater effort on the part of the Minister of Agriculture in this respect. Not long ago I said we were going to get our crops in, but I did not know how we would take the hay off, and the other crops in the fall.
It is a sad picture to go to some farms in my constituency and see old people looking after the stock, and the conditions under which they are carrying on to-day.
I have another point to bring before the committee, although it may not be quite in order. The committee on agriculture was not called until June, but in the past two days it has held meetings while the house has been in session. At one of the first meetings I said that when the chairman of the wheat board was here I would wish him to make an explanation of the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce respecting durum wheat. The other afternoon I happened to be in the house when that particular matter was explained before the committee on agriculture. I raised the question next, day, and the chairman, for whom I have great respect, said that the chairman of the wheat board had made a very full statement, one

Supply-Agriculture
which he felt would satisfy me when I read it in the proceedings of the committee. I received a copy of those proceedings this afternoon, and I wish to assure him that the statement did not satisfy me, at all. In fact, it is not as full a statement as the minister made on March 29-and that did not satisfy me, either.
Since then I have received a return dated April 14 as to the total acreage of durum wheat grown in Canada in 1942. There were some 259,000 acres, with a yield of 6,800,000 bushels. The amount of the 1942 crop marketed from August 1, 1942 to May 1, 1943 was 2,578,000 bushels. The amount exported in the same period was 526,000 bushels.
I have a return dated April 1, asking for the number of macaroni manufacturing firms in Canada, and I find that in 1941 there were twenty such firms. The total amount of flour used annually for macaroni is forty-six million pounds, which is less than one million bushels of durum wheat. Of the 1942 durum wheat crop, over two years' supply for macaroni had been delivered, and exports had been made during that period when the minister made the statement on the last day of March. According to the facts we are able to obtain, the percentage of durum wheat available over annual requirements is just as great as that of hard wheat. I know it is stated by the officials of the board that the reason for the recommendation to the government was that durum wheat delivered under the quota had been pretty well exhausted and that, in view of the prospect of meat rationing and the necessity of the encouragement of the use of other foods, it was recommended to the government that durum wheat, which is not used for bread making hut entirely for the manufacture of macaroni and other allied products, be delivered irrespective of the quota.
During the interval I have checked things in my constituency which is in southern Manitoba, and I have found that the producers there have grown considerably over 12,000 acres of duium wheat and have received a return of some 300,000 bushels. When the statement was made at the end of March, over three-quarters of that durum wheat had been marketed and there was very little left. The fact that this statement was made has created quite a change in seeding operations in southern Manitoba. This is directly the responsibility of the Department of Agriculture which ' has to do with matters of production, and since the Minister of Agriculture is a member of the wheat board, along with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Mines and Resources and the Minister of Finance-
The wheat committee, not the wheat board.

I mean the wheat
committee of the cabinet. I think the minister should enlarge upon the statement which was made. It does not bear out what we were given to understand by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the great bulk of this durum wheat is produced in southern Saskatchewan. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture is conversant with the whole picture. We may not have another opportunity to take up this matter before the seeding operations of 1944 are under way. We may be able to make a statement on the speech from the throne, but I doubt if we shall be able to go into this matter and question officials before it is too late next spring. I think the minister should enlarge upon the reasons for issuing this order, because the facts I have been able to obtain from the returns placed before the house do not bear out the situation as pictured by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

Replying to what has been said by the hon. member for Souris, I can only say that the matter to which he has referred would be dealt with entirely by the Department of Trade and Commerce and not by this department. Therefore I would hesitate to attempt to make a statement to-night without the records in front of me to show the exact situation. If it is thought wise that I should do so at some later time in the discussion, I shall be glad to look up the records and familiarize myself with them, and discuss the matter in so far as it relates to these estimates.
A number of other statements have been made with regard to the situation, and I should like to say something about them. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) appealed to me to take some stand in connection with farm labour. All I can say to him with regard to that is that we had a discussion about farm labour back in March, 1942, when it was discussed at considerable length on my estimates, as well as at other times during this session. The figures he has quoted to the committee give some indication as to what has happened as a result of the discussions which took place at that time. As has been stated already by the hon. member for Bow River, on March 1, 1939, there were 1,080,000 male family workers on the farms of Canada. In the year following, six months of which was during the first year of the war and before we became very active in making munitions or in the enlistment of men, this number was reduced to 1,065,000, or a reduction of 15,000. In the following year

there was a further reduction of 65,000, and in the year following the reduction amounted to 90,000. That was as at March 1, 1942. It was in March, 1942, that we took action to halt the increase in the number of those who were leaving the farms, and the result was that as between March 1, 1942, and March 1, 1943, only 30,000 male family workers left the farms.
What is the average yearly decrease?

I am not speaking of the average, because that does not meet the point I am making. The point is that in 1941-42 a total of 90.000 left the farms, and then, on account of the action that we took in March, 1942, only 30,000 left in the next year.
Because the surplus had already been drawn off.

Not according to the argument my hon. friend was using. He was arguing that if we went on at that rate we would have all the people off the farms. We [DOT]did not go on at that rate. Wliere there had been an increase from 65,000 to 90,000, in the following year there was a decrease to 30,000, a direct result of the action taken by the government following the discussions which had taken place in the labour committee, of which I happen to be a member.
That is stall twice as many as before the war.

We had discussions early in this session, and I think every hon. member, even those on the other side, who come from western Canada, will agree that since the discussions took place early in February there has been a marked change.
We could not stand another 30,000.

I am just replying to the statement my hon. friend made that the Minister of Agriculture ought to do something about the matter. The Minister of Agriculture did not wait until June, 1943, to. do something about it; the Minister of Agriculture acted in March, 1942, and the government, along with the Minister of Agriculture, took action. When we were not getting the results we wanted from that action I did not remain in Ottawa;
I went out to Saskatoon and met the farmers; I went to Regina and met the board.
I then came back to Ottawa and placed the situation before the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), who immediately took action. I think every hon. member from western Canada on the other side of the chamber will admit that since that action was taken, the condition has been considerably different from 
what it was before the action was taken. I make this statement to indicate that we have not been resting on our oars in connection with this whole matter.
Referring to the other question which was raised as to whether the farmers are going to the labour bureaux w-hen they are short of labour, I submit that nowhere in Hansard can it be found that during this discussion I said that the farmers ought to go to these bureaux. What I did say was that they actually do go to these bureaux. I administered the labour bureaux in Saskatchewan for five years when I was a member of that government. I know that during that period the farmers came to the labour bureaux when they were short of men, and I know they have followed that practice ever since. They have been coming to these bureaux continuously and asking for help. As for the hon. member who is just rising in his place, I am going to say something which may convince him that he had better wrait until I am through.
I was going to ask the minister if he had the figures of the percentage of farm help in the western provinces that is hired through the bureaux.

When I was west I took occasion to get the reply to the statements which were made by the hon. member for Melfort during the discussions which we had some three weeks ago. I got the report on his own municipality, and I found that, according to the statement of the secretary-treasurer-
What municipality is that?

The municipality in
which my hon. friend farms. He knows the name and number better than I do.
I doubt if the minister knows it.
I have the record, and I can place it on Hansard at any time. But my hon. friend knows what municipality it is.
It is not far from Tisdale, anyway.

It is not very far from Melfort. The facts are these, that 150 or 151 men were placed in that municipality by the individual there who acted on behalf of those who were taking care of employment in Saskatchewan. The statement which was made here was that men were asking $100 a month, and I took it from what was said that some of them were getting it. The information I got from the records was that one man had been paid $85; that that one man was an expert operator of a tractor, and that the man

who employed him was quite satisfied to pay him $85; he wanted this man for employment. Then I got the further information that a number of others were paid $75 as operators of tractors, but that the general wage paid in that municipality for farm labour was from $60 to $70 a month. That is a fairly high wage, and I would not try to build an argument on the supposition that $60 to $70 a month for farm labour in western Canada at present, and more particularly in Saskatchewan, is not a fairly high wage under all the conditions.
An lion. MEMBER: And board?

And board, yes. But I would say this, that if a farmer is going to hire a man for only the two months during which he is busy seeding, and then is going to let him go, and hire another man for two months while he is harvesting, the story is entirely different from simply saying that a man is getting $60 or $70 or, $85 a month to do a particular job. If he is to be hired through the whole summer he might be paid one wage; if he is to be hired through the whole year he might be paid another. But simply to rise in the house and say that somebody was paid $100 or $85 does not prove anything in connection with this discussion.

If I might correct the minister. I did not state that any man was paid $100 a month. I said the man was hired at $75; he asked $85 after working for two weeks,
, and the farmer agreed to give him $85; when he increased his price and wanted $100, the farmer refused to hire him at that figure. That is the statement I made. The minister has not yet answered my question as to what percentage of the farm help hired in the western provinces is hired through the employment bureaux?

It is not a question of
the percentage hired through the bureaux. I know that percentage is low. The average farmer in western Canada, like the average farmer in eastern Canada, hires his help without having to go to the. employment bureau at all. It is only when he is finding difficulty in obtaining help that he goes to the employment bureau. But if, after all those have gone to the employment bureaux who have felt inclined to go, the results are as indicated by the figures I put on Hansard, those figures do not indicate any great shortage of labour in the particular area covered by those figures, and that is all they were intended to indicate. When we go beyond that, I think every hon. member will admit that there are farms all across Canada upon which there is a shortage of labour, and the fact that any
hon. member gets half a dozen or a dozen letters in a week indicating that there is a shortage of labour on some farms is something to be expected- We have in Canada 750,000 farmers. If out of those 750,000 some few thousands are short of labour, letters will come to hon. members from those who are short of help. But I must say that, of the letters which I get with regard to shortage of labour, by far the greater number come from people whose sons have volunteered either for the armed services or for some work in munition plants or in shipyards or somewhere else; and there are a certain number too who write in on account of something which has happened in the calling up of men which is not fully understood, and about which sometimes action has been taken that should not have been taken. But I repeat what I said the other night, that by far the greater number of the cases which come to me, even yet, deal with situations which were created before the first of February last. There is the occasional one which was dealt with after that date, but that is not true of much the greater number. I quite agree that hardships are brought about by situations such as were outlined by the hon. member for Bow River. Any man who was put on a ship and sent to Britain after being fully trained must have been in the armed services before the first of February last, and was there under the conditions which existed before the last action was taken by the labour department to deal with them.
I must say, too, that a certain percentage of letters which I receive come from people who have been doing more than the country expected of them in connection with the prosecution of the war, and doing it conscientiously. For example, two or three days ago I had a letter from a woman in Saskatchewan whom I know very well, calling my attention to the fact that her son had enlisted very early in the war and was still in the service. She called my attention to the further fact that she and her husband over a considerable period of years have not been in good health -*which I also know to be true-and then she says "Our son thought that he could go over with a group of other men and clean up this fellow Hitler, get the war over and come back here to work," but, she said, "it is taking much longer than he thought. It is now going on four years, and he is still away, and we are unable to carry on longer." Well, I did what other hon. members do; I sent the letter to the military people; they have taken it up, and I am quite satisfied that in cases of that kind action is taken, and has been taken
Supply-Agriculture

regularly ever since the war started, in order to deal with such situations and make it possible for men who are in the army under those circumstances to go back to the farms and give assistance.
However, after all these individual cases that we oan bring up have been dealt with, a very large proportion of the 750,000 fanners have made no complaint whatever. If the facts were otherwise, the situation would not be what it is to-day. I have here the last figures in connection with production and the storage of farm products. They are not yet in print; but they indicate, as all the figures down to the present have indicated, that there is not this reduction in the production of farm products which is hinted here in practically every speech delivered by those who are critical of the present position.
In cheese there is a reduction in production; but in milk there is no such reduction and, after all, the foundation of all production of dairy products is milk. So that if more milk is being produced this year than last year or the year before, we are certainly not going down in our production of that particular product. There is more whole milk being consumed in Canada to-day than at any other time in our history, and the consumption is going up day by day. There may be reasons why the government might want to change that; but if they did attempt to change it, I am sure that everyone who is trying to do something to assist in seeing to it that our people, and more particularly our children, are better fed, would immediately complain about our attempting to cut down on the consumption of milk in order to get an increased production of something else.
However, in spite of the fact that cheese production is down this year as compared with last year, it is not down as compared with any other year recently in our history apart from last year; and in spite of the fact that our production is down, our exports are higher this year than they have ever been in any year since the war started. In other words, if what my hon. friend the member for Bow River is concerned about is the feeding of the British people, we are still sending them more food each year than in the previous year, and that applies not only to cheese but to pork products. And we are making preparations for sending beef, which we have never sent since the war started. We are sending, and have available, more wheat than we have been called upon to send previously. And so on. I could go through the whole list.
I say this in order to point out that the statements which were made continuously, 
and which were called to the attention of the house the other night by the Minister of Labour, have no foundation at all in fact. The hon. member for Lethbridge was holding forth on his fear that we would have shortages, and the Minister of Labour said, where, or what does he mean by shortages? If I remember the words of my hon. friend, they were to this effect: If the minister does not know what I mean by shortages, then I am not able to tell him.
His next question was, do you expect us to feed all the Chinese people? Well, now, that question was a reasonable one. Most of the discussions that are going on with regard to a possible shortage of food in Canada are related to the feeding of the whole world, and I do not think anyone in this house or in this country, who is well informed, will take such a ridiculous position as to maintain or try to maintain that a country with eleven million people, even if they were all farming, could feed even those people in China who are suffering at the present time as a result of lack of food. We are attempting to send food over to Britain in a volume which will be sufficient to keep the British people and the armed forces working out of Britain supplied with food.
Someone-I believe it was the hon. member for Bow River-said that, if necessary, we should ration ourselves down to the point where we are going short in order to save the people in Britain from going short; and that is exactly the policy the government has been following ever since the war started. From time to time we have found it necessary to ration, but I am afraid that members in this house, on account of the fact that we have never been short of anything, have an entirely wrong idea as to what rationing is put into effect for.
Britain rationed cheese last year in order to try to increase her consumption of cheese. She put the ration up to the figure of eight ouqces in an attempt to get it up to eight ounces, but it only went to five ounces.
Is that what we are doing here? Does the minister suggest that?
It might be a good thing to do it with some products which we have rationed and are now piling up in this country.
I was just asking for information.

Let me answer my hon. friends in the words of the hon. member for Lethbridge. If he does not understand it after the number of times I have explained it in the past, I am sure my explaining it again would not help him. The situation is simply

Supply-Agriculture
this, that ever since this war started we have been giving Britain all the food that we could possibly give her and at the same time keep our people fed with the minimum they require. In 1941, for example, we took all the cheese off this market during the summer months and sent it to Britain and told our people to eat something else, and they ate something else and had no difficulty in finding it.
Every year since the war started we have said to the farmers, "We do not want you to produce more butter than the people here eat", and down to last year they produced a little more than the people wanted and last year a little less than they wanted to eat, and accordingly we rationed butter. This year we have a greater amount of butter in storage than we have had over a long period of years, some four million pounds more than we had over an average of five years preceding 1940. In other words, the situation has righted itself in a very few months so far as butter production as compared with consumption is concerned. We can right any situation that may be created in connection with food in this country, so long as the situation is as it has been since the beginning of the war.
Something was said with regard to prices. It was said that we should have better returns. We have had increased returns from the production of munitions and machines of war; the companies that are producing these things have increased returns. I am not going to try to convince members of this house that farmers are getting all they ought to get in the way of prices for farm products. I do not know that anyone gets all he ought to get during war time; and if anyone is getting all he ought to get in ordinary peace times, then somebody ought to do something about it and see to it that at least we all make sacrifices during the war.
Let us look for a few moments at prices. Take butcher steers at Toronto. In 1939 the price was 86.77 per hundred and in 1942 it was $10.29 per hundred. Figure that increase, from 86.77 to $10.29. And the average of the years from 1926 to 1929 was $9.04.

The minister must, of course, make allowance, and I think he gladly will, for the fact that in 1939 the farmer who was going to feed would pay a lower price for his beef before he started to feed, whereas in the fall of 1942 he would pay a high price, and his actual returns from feeding in 1939 might be greater than his returns in 1943.

I agree. I have all the prices here and I can quote them to show the relationship. But my hon. friend, who comes
from an area where they feed cattle, knows as well as I do that when cattle are selling at present prices there is money in feeding grain to those cattle at present ceiling prices.
Provided they do not pay too much for the cattle.
That is a matter of choice which they make themselves.
There was no choice last year.
Oh, yes, there was a choice.
In my district there was none.
I will deal with that later.
They could not get the cattle except at a certain price.

The average price from 1926 to 1929 was $9.04. The average twenty-year price was $7.04, and at the present time the price fbr the same grade of cattle is $12.38. All I am pointing out is that the price has increased. There is no use in trying to give the impression that prices of other commodities have gone up and that prices of cattle have not gone up. They have gone up. Let us look at hogs. In 1939 the price was $8.91. The average for 1926-29 was $11.61, and the average for 1942 was $11.72. In other words, the price had gone up from 88.91 to $11.72, and it was eleven cents higher per hundred than the average price for 1926-29. That is on the Toronto market, and the other markets compare with that.
The price of cheese in 1939 was 12-7 cents, .and in 1942, 21-5 cents. The average price for the four years 1926 to 1929 was 18-9 cents. In other words, the price was 2-6 cents higher last year than what we call the parity basis, and there has been a difference of 8-8 cents since the war began. The jobbing price of creamery butter in 1939 was 23-8 cents, and in 1942, 35-1 cents. The parity basis was 38-2 cents. But on top of that price of 35 T cents is the bonus of 8 cents in summer and 10 cents in winter, which brings the return to a higher level than the parity basis.
And so on. I could go through all the prices for all the products and show that the government has not lost sight of the fact that there must be increased returns for farm products.
Will the minister deal with the price of wool?

I am not sure that I have that here. But I can tell my hon.

friend this, that I have the relationship between the price of wool in this country and the price in the United States, which we discussed last year, and after you have made allowance for freight and for the tariff on wool going into the United States you will find that the Canadian farmer is getting a higher return in Canada than he would get if he were permitted to sell his wool in the United States. We are paying him a subsidy on his wool, too.
That is on account of the duty.
The fact that another country puts a duty on is the reason that they have a higher price than we have. They do it to get higher prices for their own product.
That is not an excuse for our not having a better price.
It is not an excuse at all. It is a reason for our not having that higher price.
That is hardly the case with beef, is it?

There is a condition existing with regard to beef, and there is a condition existing with regard to wheat, which my hon. friend was speaking of a few moments ago. The price of wheat which prevails on the Winnipeg market is exactly the United States price less the cost of taking the wheat to the United States and after accounting for the duty and exchange. It works out to almost identically the same price that, you have on the Winnipeg grain exchange to-day. And so on. You can go through all the prices. As a matter of fact, I have gone through them to try to satisfy myself to what extent we might benefit if the United States boundary were open and we could ship our products in there, over whatever obstructions there might be against our doing so. When you take into account freight, tariff and other costs, there is nothing like the advantage in the price on the other side which some of us seem to think there might be.
What about the price to the United States farmer and the price to the Canadian farmer?

You have to take into account wages, the value of the land, overhead and so many other things before you can figure out just where the two stand on different sides of the line. Wages in the United States are higher than ours in spite of what has been said here to-night, and other

costs are similarly higher on the other side. I want to impress on the committee that the situation which was emphasized by the hon. member for Bow River is one to which the government has been alive for a considerable period of time, and it has been doing something about it. The results are something that we are not ashamed of, although we may not be satisfied with them. I think that is all I need say at the moment. We have had a long discussion on this whole question, and I would suggest to the committee that we might now carry the item.

I wish to say just a word with regard to quotas on farm machinery and farm machinery repairs. If I might speak to this question, Mr. Chairman, I think all will agree that I sat here the other evening for several hours listening to the discussion of labour problems, and I have sat. here and listened again to-night. I think, Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member will look at the figures which were put on Hansard months before, he will find very little difference between them and the figures he is now giving. In other words when you go back to December-of what year?

You still have the figures which were coming along through January and that period when, as I said before, there was considerable difficulty. Many men were called up during that period who were denied postponement, but I think everyone admits that there has been quite a change from the middle of February down to the present time.
This is up to the end of April.
If you had it by months I might be able to answer it. If you had it for January, February, March and April separately, it might indicate something.

With regard to the question of farm labour, I would suggest to the minister that larger quotas should be established in connection with new farm machinery and repair parts. We have been told lately that we have reached the peak in the manufacture of some war materials and that in some factories men are
being laid off. If this is the situation, I believe the quotas in connection with farm machinery should be increased, which would be of assistance in meeting the labour problem, particularly in the west, where I know it will be critical this fall. If we could have a larger quota of combines and some of the newer types of farm machinery made available to the farmers, it would help the situation materially. So that I would ask the minister to give serious consideration to the possibility of making available more farm machinery at this time.

I wish to raise just one point on this general item. The minister may care to say something about it in more detail under some other item, but if I am in order I should like to raise it now. [DOT] I wish to say a word about the grading of hogs. The minister may have received a number of complaints; I know that in going through the country I find that many people are perturbed over the matter of deductions in regard to hogs that are overweight. This winter I have been deluged, no doubt in common with other hon. members, with letters from people enclosing their receipt forms showing the deductions that have been made for overweight hogs. The chief complaint is that the deduction is so high for just a few pounds overweight. Farmers are not always able to ship just when they wish as a result of a number of factors into which I need not go at the present time, and when the hog is a few pounds overweight they lose $1 or $2, and, in some instances, even more. I have a number of receipts which I did not bother to bring down to the chamber;
I do not think it is worth while to put them on record, for I imagine the minister has even more of them and is probably more familiar with the situation than I am. I wonder if he has given any thought to it, because in the minds of most of the farmers the conviction remains, whether or not it is justified, that this heavy deduction for a few pounds overweight is not warranted. Many of them are quite convinced, as a matter of fact, that the packer is getting it, because some of that overweight may disappear with the dressing knife; when the hogs are being dressed they can be brought within the weight limit. I have heard the suggestion, and I pass it on to the minister for what it is worth, that instead of taking off a set amount when the weight exceeds 230 pounds, as I think it is now, or 220 pounds-

No; it is 186 pounds dressed.
Supply-Agriculture
And 230 pounds live weight?
About 240 pounds.

The suggestion is that instead of taking off fifty cents or a dollar when the hog is overweight, it might be possible to graduate the deduction, to take off perhaps twenty-five cents for the first five or ten pounds, or ten cents a pound, or something like that, so that the farmer who has gone just a few pounds over will not have the same deduction made as in the case of a farmer who has gone twelve or fifteen pounds over. I do not know whether or not the minister has given that point any consideration, but I wish he would do so.

This matter has been under discussion constantly, not only since the war began but before the war. The policy we followed before the war was that of attempting to standardize our bacon so that it would compete with Danish bacon on the British market. In order to have our bacon compete with that Danish bacon we must have 200-pound hogs, not 240 pounds, and before the war we were attempting to hold the size of the hog down to 200 pounds. It was possible for a farmer to bring in a hog weighing anywhere from 190 to 220 pounds and get B-l for it. If he had it around 200 pounds, probably he would get select for it, and receive a dollar extra instead of a discount. Since the beginning of the war, however, we have increased the weight. We are trying now to keep the weight at around 220, but we do allow them to run up to 240 and still qualify as B-l hogs, which is the price always quoted on the market.
The deduction starts at 220 pounds, does it?

No; the deduction
starts at 186 pounds dressed. If the hog is properly fed, it may run up to 240 pounds live weight and dress 186 pounds; but if it is fed in other ways, it may dress over 186 pounds without going up to the 240 pounds live weight, or it might go over the 240 pounds and still dress down to 186 pounds, depending upon how it was fed and bred. However, the general practice is to try to keep the hogs around 220 pounds, which gives a leeway of twenty pounds on either side, down to the 200 at which we tried to keep them before the war, or up to 240 pounds, to which we are allowing them to run now.
I have had some experience in this connection in marketing my own hogs. The farmer says that because the hog went up to 187

pounds when it was dressed he was docked. It was not just because it went up to 187 pounds; he could have had it anywhere between 200 and 240 pounds live weight and still be given the B-l price, or perhaps get the select price, which would mean, a dollar in addition.
The question as to whether the packer or the farmer gets the dollar is not hard to answer; all one has to do is look at the record. The policy is this, that if you produce a particularly good hog you get a dollar extra. If you produce a particularly poor hog you have $1.50 taken off. When you add together all the dollars that are paid the farmers and add together all the deductions at $1.50 taken from the farmers they just about balance each other. In other words, they are making the man who produces a poor hog help to finance the man who produces a good one, with the idea of encouraging the farmer to produce good hogs instead of poor ones. That is the general policy. It is not a matter of the packer getting more. He would be much better off if every farmer produced select hogs, and so would everyone else.
As to whether or not this is a proper policy, all one has to do is look at the records across Canada and see how the standard of hogs has been improved during the period of years the policy has been in effect. Since the war started, we have been allowing the hogs to get heavier and heavier, as I have indicated. Only last week I had a report on conditions in the British market, to the effect that during the last twelve months, by allowing these increases in weight, we have greatly reduced the standard of the bacon reaching England as compared with the Danish bacon with which we must compete when the war is over. They raised another complaint as well; they said apparently our plants have not the efficient men doing the cutting that they had previously, because quite often they find a slash in the bacon that should not be there, or other marks which indicate that the men doing the work now are not as expert as those who were doing it before the war started. In other words, the experts have gone to other work, where they can get higher pay. That all indicates that we are slipping in the standard of the bacon we are sending over to Britain at the present time. If we keep on slipping until the end of the war, and are not able to raise our standards again, before the Danish people are in a position to come into the market with their product, we shall have difficulty in continuing to hold our market in Great Britain. That is the only question involved in the matter.

Has the minister overcome the, difficulty in connection with salting?

Yes; it does reduce the standard.

The subject of man-power was discussed when the matter was raised by the hon. member for Temiscouata. From what the minister said to-night it would appear that since February the situation has somewhat improved. I was on the point of raising a matter of procedure. I would be one of the last to attempt to interfere with the consideration of any subject by 'hon. members opposite. To-night a matter was raised by the hon. member for Souris, and then we heard a reference to the farm implement and repair situation, followed by a discussion of hog grading. I pointed that out.

I raise the second point of

May I thank the minister for his answer respecting hog grading. He did not say anything about the possibility of taking a 25-cent deduction for each pound above, say, 186 pounds. We gave twenty pounds leeway.

I shall not hold up the

I think it is.
This item is statutory, and should not be discussed at this point.

I am not objecting to it. I think the minister should have a car. But what I wish to say-and I am going to be a bit bold about it, because no other person seems to have been bold enough to have mentioned it-

Perhaps my hon. friend
does not know what I am going to say. I would point out that there are other people who have to run cars, too. Those other people include members of parliament. I represent a large constituency, and I am not the only hon. member representing a large constituency. A great deal of the travelling

If my hon. friend is

Was any

The committee did not meet last year, and it is not expected they will meet this year?

Could the minister give one instance where this committee has given him advice?

On one question in which my hon. friend is very much interested, wool and sheep ahd beef and things of that kind.

No; that was decided by other authorities.
If they made that recommendation, I say it would condemn them.

It seems
rather absurd to be passing this item, even though it is only for SI ,680, if the committee does not intend to meet.

Science service.
9. Agricultural chemistry, $102,881.

This is the item, I imagine, on which the whole question of chemurgy would come up, the use of agricultural products for industrial purposes. Has the minister any statement to make as to what research is being done by the department along these lines? Some sensational results are being obtained in the United States, where they are producing grain alcohol, and from grain alcohol synthetic rubber, and also plastics, wall board and many other commodities for industrial purposes. What work is being done by the government along that line, and is any attempt being made to work out plans for post-war use of agricultural products in industry? The people on the prairies are very much interested in this question, because we recognize that after the war, if western Canada is to have a stable economy, she must develop industry, and she can only develop industry along chem-urgical lines whereby agricultural products can be used to build up some of the products in industrial demand. Early in the session the hon. member for Moose Jaw made an excellent speech on chemurgy. I understood from his speech that he was planning to move an amendment asking for half a million dollars for research to be carried on along these lines. I do not know whether he intended to move it in connection with this item or another one, but I hope he has made representations to the minister, because I know his suggestions received wide acclaim throughout the west. I hope the fact that he is becoming a rear admiral or taking an active interest in the navy is not causing him to lose interest in this particular subject.

The question which has been raised has been discussed, of course, from time to time. I do not know that this item is exactly the place to discuss it. The director of experimental farms, Doctor Archibald, is chairman of the chemurgy committee, and much of the work having to do with the possible production of rubber in Canada is carried on at the experimental farms. It would relate largely to the production of plants such as the plant which is utilized in Russia for that purpose, the producing of them on our experimental farms and trying them out; also whether it would be an advantage to attempt to make rubber from wheat through the production of alcohol, and whether we should-pursue other systems of producing it if we desire to produce it in this country at all.
The question whether we should have money for this purpose has been up every year since the war started; that is, we did not wait until

the matter was raised in the house to discuss it in council and among the different departments of government; we have been discussing it constantly. But much of the information which could be made available in connection with the question is available to us at present from the United States. Our people are working in cooperation with the Americans in the production of synthetic rubber. Any information they have is available to us through the proper officials of a different department, not the Department of Agriculture. They are working along with the Department of Munitions and Supply, and our national research council, which operates in the Department of Trade and Commerce, is carrying on research work in connection with this matter and has done so for many years. Any information which one has the other obtains and utilizes it for the purpose in hand. But I would suggest that, if this matter of rubber and the possibility of the production of rubber is to be discussed, the better place to discuss it would be upon the experimental farm estimates, because the farms are doing some work which may be helpful in this direction, and if any sum were to be brought forward at any time for the purpose it would be to implement those estimates.

Has the
minister the information so that it can be discussed under those items, or should it be discussed under Munitions and Supply, or Trade and Commerce?

In view of what is being done, it certainly should be discussed under Munitions and Supply. There is a statement published which is being sent out to those who are sending in resolutions with regard to it.
As it relates to wheat?

I think it would be better to discuss it all in one place, and the better place would be when we have the experimental farm service estimates before us. As I have said, Doctor Archibald is in charge of experimental farms and is also chairman of the chemurgy committee which is studying the question from every point of view. I think that if we discuss it while he is here we would be more in order and would get more information.
Has the minister any idea under which item the hon. member for Moose Jaw was going to bring up the matter?

I think that likely if it is brought up, that is if sums were voted, they

Food Conference
would have to be voted under supplementaries. I can say to the committee that the question has been under discussion every year since the war started, and after discussing all features of it in past years we have not brought an estimate for the purpose, for the reasons I have just stated, that there has been made available information from elsewhere, where much more has been done than we can hope to do in the years while the war is on.
Is there anywhere that the hon. member for Moose Jaw could raise the question for the purpose of the extra $500,000 item being appropriated?
He could probably raise it and say that he is in favour of it, just as many things have been raised to-night.

Some of us thought of it, but we did not care to advance it for fear it would not get the same encouragement it might be expected to receive if it were proposed by the hon. member for Moose Jaw.

It is a fact nevertheless that in the United States the federal department of agriculture have set up four experimental laboratories across the country to deal with the question of the possibility of using agricultural products for rubber. Apparently we in Canada have done nothing along similar lines. Is it felt that we shall get the benefit of the research work of the United States department of agriculture, and that there is no necessity for us doing anything here?
